2. Literature Review

Soil biodiversity underpins nutrient cycling and crop resilience across temperate systems.
Agricultural intensification has been linked to sustained declines in soil invertebrate communities (Smith, 2019).
Organic management is frequently proposed as a mitigation, though the evidence is uneven (Jones & Patel, 2020).
Earlier syntheses reported positive but heterogeneous effects across crops and climates (Okonkwo et al., 2018).
In 2019, the present trial was established on twelve paired fields.
Pairs were matched on soil texture, drainage class and elevation (six organic, six conventional).
Species richness rose by roughly 31 percent relative to paired conventional fields (García, 2021).
Microbial biomass carbon showed no consistent response across the three sampling seasons.
The pH of the sampled plots was low (4.5) in every replicate block.
Earthworm abundance was highly variable between fields and seasons (Lindqvist, 2017).
See Figure 3 and Table 2 for the full distribution of counts.
Nitrogen leaching was not measured in this study and no inference about water quality is drawn.
Comparable null results have been reported in long-term European trials (Mbeki & Duarte, 2022).
Soil temperatures ranged from 3-5 degrees during the winter sampling window.
Functional diversity metrics respond more slowly than richness to management change (Tanaka et al., 2016).
The duration of organic management is a recognised moderator of effect size (Novak, 2019b).
Tillage intensity confounds many published comparisons of management systems (Rossi, 2015).
Recent meta-analytic work has attempted to separate these effects (Haddad & Chen, 2023).
Sampling depth conventions differ substantially between the major national surveys (Weber, 2014).
Two independent groups report convergent findings for temperate cropland (Ferreira et al., 2020; Silva, 2021).

2.1 Numeric-style sources

Comparable increases in invertebrate richness are documented for temperate systems [1].
Microbial responses are considerably more variable across published trials [2].
Two syntheses disagree about the magnitude of the richness effect [3, 4].
Long-term trials show attenuation of the effect after the first decade [5].
Several regional studies report no significant change in earthworm counts [6-8].
Methodological differences explain part of the between-study heterogeneity [9].
Sampling season is a substantial and frequently uncontrolled source of variance [10].
Two recent reviews call for standardised depth and season protocols [11, 12].

References

Smith, J. (2019). Soil invertebrates under intensification. Journal of Soil Biology, 4, 1-10.
Jones, A. and Patel, R. (2020). Organic management and soil fauna. Agroecology Letters, 7, 22-31.
Okonkwo, B., Adeyemi, T., and Balogun, F. (2018). A synthesis of paired-field studies. Soil Reviews, 2, 5-19.
